title: Brahma's lotus and the dry leaf
hook: Brahma is born on a lotus, and Krishna says to live like its leaf
carry: offer the work, stay untouched like the lotus
tomorrow: a sage who loved only half of God. what happened to him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Yantra's edge, the bhupura: the goddess's home opens a gate on every side. Today, one step through the gate, and a flower older than the world.
screen: `A WALL BUILT FOR COMING HOME THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Before there's a world, there's only water, dark and still, and Vishnu asleep on it, lying on the coils of a great serpent. From his navel a stem rises, and at its top a lotus opens. In the lotus sits Brahma, the creator, with four faces, looking every way and seeing nothing but water. Where did he come from? In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, he climbs down inside the stem to find its root, searching for ages, and never reaches the bottom. So he comes back up, sits still on his flower, and turns inward. Only then does he see the Lord he grew from. And only then does he begin to make the world, seated on a lotus.
screen: `ONLY WATER.` → `A LOTUS FROM VISHNU'S NAVEL.` → `BRAHMA SEARCHES, THEN SITS STILL.`

segments.voice: That flower is everywhere in Hindu art: padma, the lotus. Brahma sits on one, Lakshmi stands on one, the Goddess is so often enthroned on one. Why? A lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean, and its leaf sheds water: drops roll right off, and nothing sticks. Krishna uses exactly that picture in the Bhagavad Gita. One who does their work as an offering to the divine, letting go of clinging to it, isn't stained by wrong, he says, any more than a lotus leaf is wet by water. That's karma yoga, the way of action. You don't run from the muddy pond of ordinary life. You stay in it, do the work, and offer it. Now step through the yantra's gate. The straight lines end and curves take over: three circles, then a ring of sixteen petals, then a ring of eight. The Saundarya Lahari counts them. The yantra seats its center on lotuses, the way an image of a god is set on a lotus seat. And that's how the tradition pictures a holy life: rising out of the mud, untouched by it.
screen: `PADMA: THE LOTUS SEAT.` · `THE LEAF THAT STAYS DRY.` · `THE GITA: OFFER THE WORK, DON'T CLING.` · `SIXTEEN PETALS, THEN EIGHT.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK. STAY UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Join your palms in front of your heart. Think of one job waiting for you today, ordinary and a bit muddy: a call, a chore, a stack of boxes. Many Hindus finish a task or a meal with two words: Krishnarpanam astu, let this be offered to Krishna. Say it softly for your one job, or, if you don't pray, simply: i offer this. Then picture a lotus leaf on dark water, and the drops rolling off.
The Sri Yantra, one step in: its lotus rings, sixteen petals and then eight, a seat for the holy that rises clean out of the mud.
For the road: offer the work, stay untouched like the lotus. Brahma was born on one. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 3.8: Brahma appears on the lotus from Vishnu's navel, searches down the stem for its root, and sees the Lord only after turning inward
Bhagavad Gita 5.10: one who acts offering their work to Brahman, giving up attachment, is not stained by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water
Saundarya Lahari 11: the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled lotuses, three circles and three lines among the parts of the Goddess's dwelling
Krishnarpanam astu: words many Hindus say to offer a task or a meal to Krishna
